did_you_know.text: Goshen was probably in the eastern Nile Delta, near the routes between Egypt and Canaan. This made it especially suitable for Jacob’s family and their livestock.
Shepherds had a low social status in ancient Egyptian society, as the story also suggests later. Their profession helped Joseph’s brothers remain a distinct group in Egypt.
Jacob, the father of a family of immigrants, blesses Pharaoh, the most powerful ruler in the region. The scene creates an interesting reversal: the elderly guest gives a blessing to the king.
The Hebrew word migurai is related to the root gur, meaning to live as a stranger or temporary resident. Jacob describes his life as one of wandering, even though he is 130 years old.
The name Rameses is sometimes associated with the later Egyptian capital Pi-Ramesse in the eastern Delta, but scholars debate the exact identification and dating of the place.
The story describes how the food crisis caused all the money in Egypt and Canaan to flow into Pharaoh’s treasury. It portrays the growing economic power of the central government during the famine.

Egypt’s priests had a special status: they received a regular allowance from Pharaoh and therefore did not have to sell their land. This shows the close connection between religious institutions and royal power.
One-fifth of the harvest is 20 percent, so the farmers kept the remaining four-fifths. The verse describes a fixed tax on crops, except for the priests’ land.
Placing a hand under the thigh was an ancient oath gesture, although its exact meaning is uncertain. Jacob uses it to emphasize that Joseph has solemnly promised to fulfill his request.

The Hebrew word mittah can mean “bed,” while the Septuagint read it as a word meaning “staff.” That is why some translations say Jacob bowed at the head of the bed, while others say he bowed over the top of his staff.
